{"id": "dc19512a-ecf2-4969-843d-7f7e719b2618", "role": "user", "content": [{"id": "tooluse_qP88yFy2ZiJD2mc2KMVOhu", "content": "[{'text': '## Documentation search results\\n\\n{\"content\":{\"result\":[{\"rank_order\":1,\"title\":\"Native Container Image Scanning in Amazon ECR | Containers\",\"context\":\"## Scanning 101\\\\n\\\\nLet us first cover the container scanning terminology to ensure we\u2019re on the same page. If you\u2019re familiar with container scanning you can skip this section.\\\\n\\\\nConceptually, scanning as a part of container security looks like this:\\\\n\\\\nWhen looking at containerized applications, we have on the one hand developers, building container images in a Continuous Integration (CI) pipeline, pushing these artifacts into ECR. On the other hand we have security operations (secops) engineers, looking after one or more ECR repositories and a number of container orchestrators, such as ECS or EKS. In this context it is important to point out that container security is a joint responsibility: developers and secops roles working together to address security along the entire cloud native supply chain. For example, developers following good practices around building secure container images, such as defining a `USER` and minimizing the attack surface by removing unnecessary build tools in the image, as well as secops verifying and enforcing runtime policies.\\\\n\\\\nFurther, we can distinguish between two kinds of scanning:\\\\n\\\\n* **Static scanning** is performed in environments prior to deployments with the implication that developers (or secops) can detect vulnerabilities before a container is launched. ECR image scanning falls under this category, that is, it enables you to scan OS packages in container images for Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVEs), a public list of known security threats, without the need to set up your own scanning infrastructure or purchase third-party scanning licenses.\\\\n* **Dynamic scanning** is executed in a runtime environment, so it\u2019s possible to identify vulnerabilities for containers running in test, QA, or production environments, making is possible to catch vulnerabilities introduced by software installed post-build as well as zero-days. For dynamic (or: runtime) container security, you have an array of options available, provided by third parties, from open source solutions such as CNCF Falco to offerings by through our AWS Container Competency Partners including Aqua Security, Trend Micro, and Twistlock.\\\\n\\\\nBased on your feedback and after evaluating different options, we decided to use the popular open source project CoreOS Clair in our ECR image scanning feature to carry out the static analysis of vulnerabilities. We\u2019ve extended the ECR API, the AWS CLI and SDKs with image scanning functionality and implemented a scalable and reliable managed service for you to use in a CI pipeline or via the command line.\\\\n\\\\nLet\u2019s start with a concrete, real-world use case: scheduled re-scans of container images in ECR\",\"url\":\"https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/containers/amazon-ecr-native-container-image-scanning/\"},{\"rank_order\":2,\"title\":\"Container image scanning\",\"context\":\"# Container image scanning\\\\n\\\\nImage Scanning is an automated vulnerability assessment feature that helps improve the security of your application\u2019s container images by scanning them for a broad range of operating system vulnerabilities.\\\\n\\\\nCurrently, the Amazon Elastic Container Registry (ECR) is only able to scan Linux container image for vulnerabilities. However; there are third-party tools which can be integrated with an existing CI/CD pipeline for Windows container image scanning.\\\\n\\\\n* Anchore\\\\n* PaloAlto Prisma Cloud\\\\n* Trend Micro - Deep Security Smart Check\\\\n\\\\nTo learn more about how to integrate these solutions with Amazon Elastic Container Repository (ECR), check:\\\\n\\\\n* Anchore, scanning images on Amazon Elastic Container Registry (ECR)\\\\n* PaloAlto, scanning images on Amazon Elastic Container Registry (ECR)\\\\n* TrendMicro, scanning images on Amazon Elastic Container Registry (ECR)\",\"url\":\"https://docs.aws.amazon.com/eks/latest/best-practices/windows-images.html\"},{\"rank_order\":3,\"title\":\"Image security\",\"context\":\"### Scan images for vulnerabilities regularly\\\\n\\\\nLike their virtual machine counterparts, container images can contain\\\\nbinaries and application libraries with vulnerabilities or develop\\\\nvulnerabilities over time. The best way to safeguard against exploits is\\\\nby regularly scanning your images with an image scanner. Images that are\\\\nstored in Amazon ECR can be scanned on push or on-demand (once during a\\\\n24 hour period). ECR currently supports\\\\ntwo\\\\ntypes of scanning - Basic and Enhanced. Basic scanning leverages\\\\nClair an open source image scanning\\\\nsolution for no cost.\\\\nEnhanced\\\\nscanning uses Amazon Inspector to provide automatic continuous scans\\\\nfor additional cost. After an\\\\nimage is scanned, the results are logged to the event stream for ECR in\\\\nEventBridge. You can also see the results of a scan from within the ECR\\\\nconsole. Images with a HIGH or CRITICAL vulnerability should be deleted\\\\nor rebuilt. If an image that has been deployed develops a vulnerability,\\\\nit should be replaced as soon as possible.\\\\n\\\\nKnowing where images with vulnerabilities have been deployed is\\\\nessential to keeping your environment secure. While you could\\\\nconceivably build an image tracking solution yourself, there are already\\\\nseveral commercial offerings that provide this and other advanced\\\\ncapabilities out of the box, including:\\\\n\\\\n* Grype\\\\n* Palo\\\\n Alto - Prisma Cloud (twistcli)\\\\n* Aqua\\\\n* Kubei\\\\n* Trivy\\\\n* Snyk\\\\n\\\\nA Kubernetes validation webhook could also be used to validate that\\\\nimages are free of critical vulnerabilities. Validation webhooks are\\\\ninvoked prior to the Kubernetes API. They are typically used to reject\\\\nrequests that don\u2019t comply with the validation criteria defined in the\\\\nwebhook.\\\\nThis\\\\nis an example of a serverless webhook that calls the ECR\\\\ndescribeImageScanFindings API to determine whether a pod is pulling an\\\\nimage with critical vulnerabilities. If vulnerabilities are found, the\\\\npod is rejected and a message with list of CVEs is returned as an Event\",\"url\":\"https://docs.aws.amazon.com/eks/latest/best-practices/image-security.html\"}]}}\\n\\n## Recent AWS announcements (What\\'s New)\\n\\nNewer than your training data may be. When these conflict with the documentation results above or with what you remember, prefer the most recent dated source.\\n\\n{\"content\":{\"result\":[{\"rank_order\":1,\"title\":\"Amazon ECR enhanced scanning now surfaces image use status - AWS\",\"context\":\"Amazon Elastic Container Registry (ECR) enhanced scanning now provides information on how images are used on Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (EKS) and Amazon Elastic Container Service (ECS). This includes the last used date, the number of clusters using the image, and the ARNs of the clusters. This data can help prioritize vulnerability remediation for actively used images. ECR enhanced scanning is an integration with Amazon Inspector, which scans container images for operating system and programming language package vulnerabilities. Users can now identify when an image was last used, the number of clusters using it, and which clusters are running it with ARNs using the ECR or Inspector consoles and APIs. Make sure that the [add-on version is compatible with the Kubernetes cluster version](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/eks/latest/userguide/managing-vpc-cni.html#vpc-cni-latest-available-version)\",\"url\":\"https://repost.aws/knowledge-center/eks-troubleshoot-vpc-cni-add-on\"},{\"rank_order\":2,\"title\":\"Amazon VPC CNI\",\"context\":\"### Routinely Upgrade CNI Version\\\\n\\\\nThe VPC CNI is backward compatible.
